paragraphs: The first and most intense passion that the equality of conditions produces is, I hardly need say, the love of that same equality. My readers will therefore not be surprised that I speak of it before all others. Everyone has noticed that in our time, and especially in France, this passion for equality is gaining ground in the human heart every day. People have said a hundred times that our contemporaries are far more ardently and stubbornly attached to equality than to freedom. But since I do not find that the causes of this fact have been analyzed enough, I shall try to point them out.

We can imagine an extreme point at which freedom and equality would meet and merge. Suppose that all the members of the community take part in the government, and that each of them has an equal right to do so. Since no one differs from his fellows, no one can exercise tyrannical power. Men will be perfectly free because they will all be entirely equal, and they will be perfectly equal because they will be entirely free. Democratic nations tend toward this ideal state. It is the most complete form that equality can take on earth, but there are a thousand others that, though not as perfect, are no less dear to those nations.

The principle of equality can be established in civil society without prevailing in the political world. Men may have equal rights to indulge in the same pleasures, to enter the same professions, to frequent the same places — in a word, to live in the same manner and seek wealth by the same means — although they do not all take an equal share in the government. A kind of equality may even be established in the political world where there is no political freedom at all. A man may be the equal of all his countrymen except one, who is the master of all without distinction and who chooses the agents of his power equally from among them all. One could easily imagine several other combinations in which very great equality is joined to institutions that are more or less free, or even to institutions wholly without freedom. Men cannot become absolutely equal unless they are entirely free, and so equality, pushed to its furthest extent, may merge with freedom. Even so, there is good reason to distinguish the one from the other. The taste men have for liberty and the taste they have for equality are in fact two different things, and I am not afraid to add that among democratic nations they are two unequal things.

On close inspection, we see that every age has some particular and dominant fact to which all others are connected. This fact almost always gives birth to some fruitful idea or ruling passion, which draws all the feelings and opinions of the time to itself and carries them along in its course. It is like a great stream toward which each of the surrounding rivulets seems to flow. Freedom has appeared in the world at different times and in various forms. It has not been bound exclusively to any social condition, and it is not confined to democracies. Freedom therefore cannot be the distinguishing characteristic of democratic ages. The particular and dominant fact that marks those ages as its own is the equality of conditions, and the ruling passion of men in those periods is the love of this equality. Do not ask what strange charm the men of democratic ages find in being equal, or what special reasons they may have for clinging so stubbornly to equality rather than to the other advantages that society offers them. Equality is the distinguishing characteristic of the age they live in, and that alone is enough to explain why they prefer it to all the rest.

But apart from this reason, there are several others that will at all times habitually lead men to prefer equality to freedom. If a people could ever succeed in destroying the equality that prevails within it, or even in reducing it, it could do so only through long and laborious effort. Its social condition would have to be changed, its laws abolished, its opinions replaced, its habits altered, its mores corrupted. Political liberty, on the other hand, is more easily lost: to neglect to hold it fast is to let it slip away. Men therefore cling to equality not only because it is dear to them but also because they believe it will last forever.

Even the narrowest and most unthinking minds can see that political freedom, in its excesses, may endanger the peace, the property, and the lives of individuals. But only attentive and clear-sighted men perceive the dangers with which equality threatens us, and they usually avoid pointing them out. They know that the calamities they fear are remote, and they comfort themselves that these will fall only on future generations, about whom the present generation thinks very little. The evils that freedom sometimes brings are immediate. Everyone can see them, and everyone is affected by them more or less. The evils that extreme equality may produce come to light slowly. They creep gradually into the social frame, they are noticed only at intervals, and by the time they become most violent, habit has already stopped people from feeling them. The advantages of freedom show themselves only over time, and it is always easy to mistake the cause from which they come. The advantages of equality are instantaneous, and they can always be traced back to their source. Political liberty bestows exalted pleasures from time to time on a certain number of citizens. Equality confers a number of small enjoyments on every man every day. The charms of equality are felt at every moment and are within everyone’s reach. The noblest hearts are not insensible to them, and the most vulgar souls delight in them. The passion that equality produces must therefore be at once strong and general. Men cannot enjoy political liberty without paying for it with some sacrifices, and they never obtain it without great exertion. But the pleasures of equality offer themselves freely. Each of the small incidents of life seems to bring them about, and to taste them nothing is required but to live.

Democratic nations are fond of equality at all times, but there are certain epochs when their passion for it swells to the height of fury. This happens at the moment when the old social system, long under threat, completes its own destruction after a last internal struggle, and the barriers of rank are finally thrown down. At such times men pounce on equality as their booty, and they cling to it as to a precious treasure they fear to lose. The passion for equality penetrates men’s hearts on every side, spreads there, and fills them entirely. Do not tell them that by surrendering blindly to one exclusive passion they risk their dearest interests: they are deaf. Do not show them freedom slipping from their grasp while they are looking the other way: they are blind — or rather, they can see only one thing in the universe worth desiring.

What I have said applies to all democratic nations. What I am about to say concerns the French alone. Among most modern nations, and especially among all those of the Continent of Europe, the taste for freedom and the idea of it began to exist and to spread only when social conditions were tending toward equality, and as a consequence of that very equality. Absolute kings were the most effective levelers of ranks among their subjects. Among these nations equality came before freedom. Equality was therefore a long-established fact while freedom was still a novelty. Equality had already created customs, opinions, and laws of its own when freedom, alone and for the first time, came into actual existence. So freedom was still only a matter of opinion and taste, while equality had already crept into the habits of the people, taken hold of their mores, and given a particular turn to the smallest actions of their lives. Is it any wonder that the men of our own time prefer the one to the other?

I think that democratic communities have a natural taste for freedom. Left to themselves, they will seek it, cherish it, and regret any loss of it. But their passion for equality is ardent, insatiable, incessant, and invincible. They call for equality in freedom, and if they cannot obtain that, they still call for equality in slavery. They will endure poverty, servitude, and barbarism, but they will not endure aristocracy. This is true at all times, and especially true in our own. Any men or powers who try to fight this irresistible passion will be overthrown and destroyed by it. In our age, freedom cannot be established without it, and despotism itself cannot reign without its support.
